title: The king and the handmaid
hookLine: a king loves a young woman who falls ill, and no doctor can help (Masnavi 1.36ff)

lines: A KING SEES A YOUNG WOMAN.
cards: Tired, so more coffee. Unhappy at work, so more hours. Lonely, so another app.

Sometimes the fix becomes the problem, and each round makes things a little worse. Rumi's first story in the Masnavi starts right there. A king out hunting sees a young woman, a servant girl, and falls in love.
He buys her and brings her home. Almost at once she falls ill, and she keeps getting worse. Today, the king and the handmaid.

teach.h: A KING BUYS A SERVANT GIRL.
teach.b: First, the setting, honestly. In Rumi's world a king could buy a servant girl, and the story takes that for granted. It's hard to hear today, and it's fine to feel that.
Rumi tells it as a parable about the soul, not a model of love.

teach.h: THE PHYSICIANS FORGET: IF GOD WILLS.
teach.b: The king gathers the best physicians from everywhere: save her, and I'll give you anything. They're confident.
Each of us, they say, has a cure for every pain; we'll heal her. And Rumi notices something. Out of pride, they don't say, if God wills.

It sounds tiny, but behind it stands a verse of the Quran, in Pickthall's translation: "And say not of anything: Lo! I shall do that tomorrow, Except if Allah will." Rumi doesn't mean just saying the words.
He means the humility inside them: knowing the outcome isn't fully yours. The physicians try remedy after remedy, and every cure does the opposite of what it should. The girl grows thin as a hair.
The king weeps. Finally he sees it: this isn't working.
He runs barefoot to the mosque, weeps on the prayer mat until it's wet, and prays for help. The answer is tomorrow's story. The physicians weren't bad at medicine.
They were sure of themselves, and they were treating the wrong illness.
Sometimes the honest first step is the king's plain admission: it isn't working.

how: The story of the king and the handmaid is the first tale of the Masnavi, and Sufi teachers traditionally read it as an allegory of the soul, its false loves and its true healer.

o: a Sufi prayer said at the mosque
a Persian book of medical cures

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: falls in love on a hunt
falls ill, grows thin as a hair
forget to say if God wills
where the king weeps and prays

s: the physicians fail because they know no medicine
they're skilled, but proud, and treating the wrong illness.
Rumi says the words alone aren't the point
he means the humility inside if God wills, not just saying it.
the story is Rumi's model of good love
he tells it as a parable about the soul, not as a model for how to love.

games.q: you're the king. every cure the finest physicians try makes her worse. what do you do?
o: run barefoot to the mosque and pray.
games.why: the king admits it isn't working, runs barefoot to the mosque, and weeps on the prayer mat. the answer comes in tomorrow's story.

practice: Think of something you keep doing to feel better that doesn't really help: scrolling to calm down, working late to feel safe, snacking when you're lonely, staying busy so you won't feel sad.
Don't scold yourself; just see it clearly, the way the king finally did, and say inside: it isn't working. Then sit quietly with not knowing what would.

wordCard.voice: Masnavi, Rumi's book of stories: its first tale, where proud physicians' cures only make the dying girl worse. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: if God wills. the words the proud physicians left out.

carryVoice: Your line: it isn't working. The king is still on the prayer mat, and the story isn't over. See you tomorrow.
